read_at_rule: Every time in this file is a fact about a past read. Nothing here states a cadence this project promises to keep or a latency a reader may rely on.
nothing_derived_rule: This file carries no regulation, season, date, limit, fee or sentence from any source. It carries the address this project re-read, the moment it re-read it, the digest of the bytes it compared against, and one of three words.
fold_rule: A domain's result is the worst of its own sources' results, worst first: changed_pending_review, then unreachable, then unchanged. That is the only reduction performed anywhere in this file. No value from any source appears here.
changed_never_moves_a_value: A source that changed shows no new value anywhere in this app. The redline and promote path is the only thing that moves a value and it ends at a person; until it does, this app shows the text it last checked and says a change is under review.

cadence.basis: This is the cadence on which this project RE-READS its sources. It is not a claim about how often any source changes, and no screen states one.

domains_not_checked.reason: The State's beach programme catalog, read from data.ca.gov's CKAN API, which answers with a fresh envelope per request and no revision marker.

The State's monitoring-station catalog, read from the same data.ca.gov CKAN API and for the same reason as `beach_health`: the endpoint answers a fresh envelope per request and publishes no revision marker, so a byte comparison would report a change every morning.
The Coastal Commission's YourCoast API answers a fresh JSON document per request and publishes no revision marker.

Quoted statute. leginfo.legislature.ca.gov publishes `Disallow: /`, so the Penal Code and Fish & Game Code sections are read by a person through a manual lane and this project does not scrape them. The federal restoration records carry their own `recheck_by` dates and the builder refuses one that has passed.

The hunter-education and document rules are quoted from CDFW pages and PDFs that `curated/editions.json` records as publishing no edition marker of any kind (`edition_state: unknown`), and no watch family in `watch.py` reads them. A byte comparison against a DotNetNuke page would report a change every morning — the reason `check_html_tables` compares PARSED TABLES — and these pages carry prose rather than tables. Declared here so the app says the check does not cover it.
CDFW's SHARE and PLM pages are read through a curation lane that ends at a person, because an application window is a deadline and a deadline read wrongly is worse than one read late.

The weekly rotation has not yet completed its first full pass over the 1,560 records: 3 of 7 nights have been read. A domain row is published when every seventh of the directory has been re-read at least once, because with part of the rotation done the honest summary is not 'checked' — the rest has not been looked at since the research pass. Until then the app falls back to this file's own clock and says the daily check does not cover it.

The BLM, USFS and CDFW ownership layers are ArcGIS query endpoints whose `editingInfo` this project has not established as published and trustworthy for every one of the six services. A re-read that compared whole GeoJSON payloads would call a re-projection a regulation change, which is the one thing a receipt may never do. Declared here so the app says the check does not cover it.

Bundled zone GEOMETRY from api.weather.gov/zones. The endpoint answers a fresh JSON document per request and publishes no revision marker, so a byte comparison would report a change every morning. Its clock is 365 days for the same reason.

Derived from the layers this app ships, and re-derived from `dataset/current` by `tests/test_planner_coverage.py` on every run — a far harder gate than a clock. What ages here is a curatorial judgement about the shipped dataset, not anything published anywhere. The row is `non_regulatory` and is never badged.
CDFW's Shark Incident Database, published as a zip on data.cnra.ca.gov. The archive is re-generated on download, so its bytes move without the records moving.

NOAA ENC Direct again, and the same ArcGIS-payload problem `spear_structures` carries: the three scale bands publish no `editingInfo` at all (every layer's metadata answers `editingInfo: null`, read 2026-09-21), so there is no edit date to compare and a re-query returns a freshly generated document whose bytes move without the chart moving. What CAN be re-read is inside the file: every record carries NOAA's own source date for the features it was measured from, so a reader sees the survey vintage per spot rather than a claim about when this pipeline last asked.

R59 Lane U. A CURATED draft with no fetch command behind it: 49 notes read off published agency pages by R59 Lane F on 2026-09-22, each carrying that page's own URL and read date, plus the MPA context rows and four derived seabed fields. Nothing polls those pages, and nothing should until the owner has confirmed the draft — the row ships `owner_review` and Settings badges it as a draft.

What a reader re-reads instead is on the card: every note prints its publisher and the day it was read, so the age of a statement about a beach is visible per statement rather than as one claim about the file. Four notes carry `time_sensitive` in the data — an access restriction, a seasonal closure and two seasonal notices — and they are what a person re-reads first.

R59 Lane S. Four catalogues from three hosts, and none of them publishes a change detector this watch could poll. CDIP's THREDDS catalogue is a directory listing that is regenerated on every request; its MOP point set is an attribute of two model aggregates; the CeNCOOS/SCCOOS ERDDAP nodes answer a search with a freshly built table; and CO-OPS' harmonic constants carry no ETag and no modified date on the mdapi path. A re-query would return bytes that move without anything having changed, which is the `spear_structures` problem exactly.

What can be re-read is INSIDE the file, and it is better than a poll: every station carries NOAA's own `comments` string naming the analysis its constants came from — "average of 6 one-year lsqha; 2007 - 2012" at La Jolla — and every resolution carries the metres to the instrument, so a reader sees the vintage and the distance per spot rather than a claim about when this pipeline last asked. The READINGS these catalogues point at are checked on their own clocks and not this one: the CDIP buoy and the pier station are fetched live per spot, and the MOP nowcast rides `mop_nearshore_current`'s threshold.
NOAA ENC, BOEM and CDFW reef and pier layers — the same ArcGIS-payload problem `land_status` carries, across three organisations.
What ages here is a LICENCE STATEMENT, not a photograph, and re-reading one is a person's judgement about words a licensor wrote. `non_regulatory`; never badged.
NOAA's CO-OPS station metadata API and the NDBC station table. Both answer fresh documents per request; the NDBC table is a plain-text listing with no marker.

This app's own editorial content rather than anybody's published document, so there is no source to re-read. The row is `non_regulatory` and is never badged: an age warning over a fishing tip reads as 'these regulations may be out of date', which is the frame the tips design exists to keep clean.

A cited factor table: every row is a UNIT, a citation and a disclaimer read off a published document by a person, on an annual cadence. No threshold and no regulation value lives in it — the only threshold this app compares against is the number the reader saved — so there is nothing here a watch could watch.
DERIVED from the bundled catalogs it joins and fresher than none of them. It has no source of its own to re-read.
The Forest Service alert pages are read per-forest through a manual lane; no fetcher runs in CI.
The Ocean Plan and the bacteria provisions are State Water Board PDFs, re-read by a person when the Board adopts an amendment. They are the one family in this app the owner has personally signed off.
